source: Schoenfeld (1992) Learning to think mathematically (Handbook chapter)
finding: Students hold a 'five-minute' belief: if you understood the material, any assigned problem takes about five minutes or less. Listed as one of seven typical student beliefs.
numbers: Table 3 lists seven beliefs; this is one.
quote: Students who have understood the mathematics they have studied will be able to solve any assigned problem in five minutes or less.
limits: Rests on observation of school exercise sets and a questionnaire; the chapter is a review, not a replication.
agent_relevance: Our agent has no such human belief by training, but it may copy a 'quick answer' prior. A guardrail should set an explicit time and effort budget for hard problems.

source: Schoenfeld (1988, as cited in 1992) questionnaire on homework time
finding: Grades 9-12 students said a typical homework problem should take about 2 minutes if you understand it, and that about 12 minutes is the longest sensible time before a problem is impossible.
numbers: Mean 2.2 min (n=221) for typical problem; mean 11.7 min (n=227) for 'impossible' cut-off; 12 high school classes.
limits: Self-report in one school district; open-ended item; read here only through the 1992 chapter quotation.
agent_relevance: Gives a human anchor for giving-up time. An agent could log how long it persists before abandoning a line and compare with problem difficulty.

source: Schoenfeld (1988, as cited in 1992) year-long geometry class observation
finding: Exercise-style teaching taught the five-minute belief. In a dozen classes no task was a real problem; a unit test had 25 problems, about 2 min 10 s each; homework sets had 28, 45, 18, 27, 30 items.
numbers: 12 classes observed a full school year; 25 test items; 2 min 10 s per item.
limits: Single school; observational; mechanism is inferred, not tested by manipulation.
agent_relevance: Training data of exercises with short solutions may teach the same time prior to LLMs; supply long-horizon problems in test-time scaffolds.

source: Schoenfeld (1992 review of 1985 video corpus) wild goose chase
finding: About 60 percent of solution attempts by college and high school students on unfamiliar problems were 'read, decide quickly, pursue come hell or high water'. A quick wrong decision, if never reconsidered, guarantees failure.
numbers: Over 100 videotapes; roughly 60% such attempts pre-course.
quote: read, make a decision quickly, and pursue that direction come hell or high water
limits: Video coding by Schoenfeld; informal reporting in the chapter; not independently replicated here.
agent_relevance: Direct human analogue of an LLM committing to the first plan. Supports a forced re-evaluation operator at fixed checkpoints.

source: Schoenfeld (1992 review) problem-solving course effect on wild goose chases
finding: After Schoenfeld's problem-solving course, the 'jump in and pursue no matter what' attempts fell from 60% to under 20%, with a concomitant rise in success.
numbers: 60% to <20% of attempts; success rise reported without a single number in this passage.
limits: Instructor-run course, small groups, no matched control reported in this passage.
agent_relevance: Shows the pattern is trainable with control-focused instruction. For an agent, prompts that make monitoring explicit may play the same role.

source: Lester, Garofalo & Kroll (1989) metacognition instruction in grade 7 (as reported in Schoenfeld 1992)
finding: Metacognitive instruction in two seventh-grade classes (teacher as external monitor, modelling executive behaviour) used 16.1 hours over 12 weeks, about 35.7% of class time.
numbers: 16.1 h; 12 weeks; 35.7% of math class time; one regular and one advanced class.
limits: Described secondhand; effect sizes not given in the passage read.
agent_relevance: Cost of the intervention is large for humans; for an agent, a monitor step is cheap. Effect size should be checked in the original report.

source: Carey, Hill, Devine & Szucs (2016) The Chicken or the Egg?
finding: Evidence on the direction of maths anxiety (MA) and performance conflicts. Longitudinal and learning-disability studies support the Deficit Theory; anxiety-manipulation studies support Debilitating Anxiety. Authors propose a reciprocal vicious cycle.
numbers: Cites Hembree (1990) r=-0.27 and Ma (1999) r=-0.34 for MA and performance.
limits: Mini review; no new data; few longitudinal studies at the time.
agent_relevance: Do not assume affect is only a cause or only an effect. For an agent, 'failure raises doubt, doubt raises failure' loops may exist in long traces.

source: Park, Ramirez & Beilock (2014) Role of expressive writing in math anxiety (cited in Carey 2016)
finding: Writing freely about emotions before a maths test raised performance in high-anxiety students, which supports interference by intrusive worry.
numbers: No numbers read; known only as cited in Carey et al. (2016).
limits: Not opened. Replication status not checked this session.
agent_relevance: Analogue: a short 'offload worries' step before a hard problem. Unproven for LLMs.

source: Faust, Ashcraft & Fleck (1996) timing and MA (cited in Carey 2016)
finding: MA is less linked to maths performance when tests are untimed, which suggests anxiety hurts mainly under time pressure.
numbers: Not read; cited as supporting cognitive interference.
limits: Not opened; secondhand.
agent_relevance: Time limits may interact with affect; for an agent, token or time budgets may create analogous pressure.

source: Beilock & Carr (2005); Ramirez et al. (2013) via Carey 2016: working memory and pressure
finding: High-working-memory students, who use memory-heavy strategies, are impaired more under pressure than those who use simpler strategies.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened; cited secondhand.
agent_relevance: Counter-intuitive: stronger solvers can be hurt more. Check whether bigger LLMs react more to pressure prompts.

source: Caviola et al. (2022) Math performance and academic anxiety forms: meta-analysis on 906,311 participants
finding: Maths anxiety correlates negatively with maths performance across 121 studies and 169 independent samples.
numbers: r = -.30, 95% CI [-.32, -.28]; I2 = 98%; tau = 0.15; trim-and-fill added no studies for the overall estimate.
limits: Mostly cross-sectional; two samples had over 250,000 people; heterogeneity is extreme; causation unsettled.
agent_relevance: Anchor effect size for 'affect hurts maths' in humans: small to medium, not large.

source: Caviola et al. (2022) moderators of the MA-math link
finding: Task type and age moderate the link slightly. Basic knowledge shows the weakest link; gender is not a significant moderator.
numbers: Basic knowledge r=-.22 [-.34,-.09] (10 studies); applied math r=-.31 (78 studies); arithmetic r=-.25 (43); grades r=-.31 (38); children r=-.31 vs adults r=-.25 (-.22 after trim-and-fill); gender B=.09, p=.075 (males r=-.20, females r=-.29, 16 studies).
limits: Gender data came from only 16 studies; adult estimate shrinks after correction for publication bias.
agent_relevance: Affect matters more on complex applied problems than on recall. The scaffold should add care on hard multi-step items, not on easy lookups.

source: Caviola et al. (2022) working memory mediation
finding: The popular claim that anxiety hurts maths by eating working memory is weakly supported in meta-analytic data.
numbers: MA-WM r=-.18 [-.24,-.13] (23 studies, N=2,695); verbal WM r=-.19, spatial r=-.16, short-term memory r=-.14; indirect effect of MA on maths via WM B<=.05 for all samples, 'negligible'.
limits: Mediation built from pooled correlations; many studies measured WM differently.
agent_relevance: Rival to attentional-control theory is not settled. Do not assume that clearing context fixes affect-like failures.

source: Barroso et al. (2021) Meta-analysis of math anxiety and math achievement (abstract via search snippet)
finding: Largest earlier meta-analysis: small-to-moderate negative link between math anxiety and achievement from childhood through adulthood.
numbers: r = -.28 from 747 effect sizes, studies 1992-2018 (as reported in a search summary; not opened).
limits: Not opened; counts of studies differ between summaries.
agent_relevance: Agrees with the Caviola r=-.30 within rounding; two meta-analyses support a stable r about -.3.

source: Yeager et al. (2019) National Study of Learning Mindsets
finding: Pre-registered national randomised test of an under-one-hour online growth-mindset module for ninth graders. Lower-achieving students gained a little in GPA.
numbers: Lower achievers n=6,320, k=65 schools: B=0.10 grade points (95% CI 0.04-0.16), SMD 0.11, p=0.001. Higher achievers B=0.01 (n=6,170). Interaction B=0.09, n=12,490.
limits: Small effect; only the pre-registered subgroup shows it; authors are the intervention developers.
agent_relevance: Even the best-run affect-belief intervention gives about 0.1 SD. Expect small gains from belief-style prompts.

source: Yeager et al. (2019) advanced maths enrolment and peer norms
finding: Intervention raised advanced maths (algebra II or higher) enrolment in 10th grade, and effects depended on peer norms that support challenge-seeking.
numbers: Full cohort n=6,690, k=41: +3 percentage points (33% to 36%, 9% relative), p=0.001. Lower 75% of schools: +2 points (p=0.045).
limits: Peer-norm moderator was a pre-specified hypothesis but heterogeneity is hard to verify outside this sample.
agent_relevance: Context moderates belief effects. For an agent the 'context' is the prompt and scaffold, so a belief message may work only with supportive structure.

source: Macnamara & Burgoyne (2023) Do growth mindset interventions impact achievement? (preprint)
finding: Systematic review of 63 studies finds a small overall effect that vanishes after publication-bias correction and for the best studies. Authors with a financial interest reported larger effects.
numbers: All studies N=97,672: 0.05 [0.02,0.09]; mindset-changed only 13 studies N=18,355: 0.04 [-0.01,0.10]; best evidence 6 studies N=13,571: 0.02 [-0.06,0.10].
limits: Preprint version; the published version may differ in wording; critics argue the strict filter drops valid studies.
agent_relevance: Strong caution: belief interventions have near-zero reliable effect on grades. Do not over-invest in motivational wording for the agent.

source: Sisk et al. (2018) mindset meta-analyses (as reported in Macnamara & Burgoyne)
finding: Mindset relates weakly to achievement, and interventions help a little, but not when the manipulation check succeeded.
numbers: Study 1: 129 studies, N=365,915, mindset explains about 1% of variance. Study 2: 38 samples, N=57,155, d=0.08 [0.02,0.14].
limits: Read only via Macnamara & Burgoyne; original not opened.
agent_relevance: Mindset itself, as a belief held, is a poor predictor.

source: Li & Bates (2019) mindset vs effort encouragement (as reported in Macnamara & Burgoyne)
finding: Failed replication of mindset effects. A fixed-mindset message plus effort encouragement did as well as effort encouragement alone.
numbers: Large-sample follow-ups (n=211, 222, 246, 586) found no significant mindset-grade link.
limits: Not opened; secondhand description.
agent_relevance: Suggests the active ingredient is effort encouragement, which maps to prompts like 'keep going on this path'.

source: Li, Wang et al. (2023) EmotionPrompt
finding: Adding an emotional cue to a prompt raised LLM scores on 45 tasks across Flan-T5, Vicuna, Llama 2, BLOOM, ChatGPT, GPT-4.
numbers: Relative gain +8.00% on Instruction Induction (24 tasks) and +115% on BIG-Bench (21 tasks); human study 106 participants, +10.9% mean on performance, truthfulness, responsibility.
quote: This is very important to my career.
limits: BIG-Bench base scores were low so 115% relative is a small absolute move; zero-shot only on BIG-Bench; no math-only benchmark isolated.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM counterpart to the 'affect helps' claim. Cheap to try, but gains are task and model dependent.

source: Li, Wang et al. (2023) EmotionPrompt limits
finding: Best stimulus varies by task set; stacking more stimuli can reduce gains. Emotional prompts made answers more definitive in the two reported failure cases.
numbers: EP02 best on Instruction Induction (6.06% above the worst); EP06 best on BIG-Bench; performance can fall when more stimuli are added.
limits: Authors report no systematic robustness test across prompt phrasing.
agent_relevance: Pressure cues may raise overconfidence. Pair any pressure with a verification step.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Do NOT think that much for 2+3=? Overthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: Reasoning models spend huge compute on trivial questions, often finding the right answer early and then re-checking. Self-training cut tokens at no accuracy cost.
numbers: For '2+3', o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models; QwQ-32B-Preview on MATH500: tokens cut 48.6% with accuracy kept; 2 to 4 solution rounds in 76-80% of QwQ cases.
limits: Tested on QwQ-32B-Preview and DeepSeek-R1 families; the fix needs fine-tuning, not just prompting.
agent_relevance: The opposite failure to the five-minute belief: too much persistence on easy items. The scaffold needs a stop rule as well as a continue rule.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts are all over the place: underthinking
finding: Reasoning models switch lines of thought too often on hard maths, abandoning promising paths. Incorrect answers had more thought switches than correct ones.
numbers: AIME2024: DeepSeek-R1-671B about 59.3 thoughts in wrong answers vs 12.6 in right (read from figure text, attribution of columns uncertain). TIP decoding: QwQ-32B-Preview Pass@1 38.3 to 44.1 on AIME2024; MATH500-Hard 83.1 to 83.7; GPQA Diamond 57.6 to 59.1.
limits: Figure numbers parsed from PDF text; penalty tuned on AIME 2022-23; DeepSeek-R1 with TIP gained only 73.8 to 74.8.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM analogue of giving up after minutes (Schoenfeld). A switching penalty is a decoding-level persistence knob; a scaffold may do it by requiring a reason to abandon a path.

source: Wang et al. (2025) TIP sensitivity to penalty size
finding: Persistence helps only up to a point. Longer or stronger penalties can hurt.
numbers: At low strength (alpha=3), duration beta 300 to 600 raised accuracy 35.2% to 39.8% on the dev set; at alpha=20, beta beyond 300 lowered accuracy. Chosen alpha=3, beta=600.
limits: Dev-set results on AIME 2022-23 only.
agent_relevance: Persistence needs a ceiling. Matches the human boundary: neither give up at five minutes nor chase wild geese forever.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking
finding: On controlled puzzles, reasoning models raise thinking effort with complexity, then reduce it near collapse despite spare token budget, an 'effort giving-up' pattern.
numbers: Three regimes: standard LLMs better at low complexity; reasoning models better at moderate; both collapse to near-zero at high. In failures the model fixates on an early wrong answer and wastes budget.
limits: Puzzle environments only; later critiques about output limits were not verified here.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM mirror of 'stop trying when hard'. A scaffold should keep budget alive and force re-planning when effort drops.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: simple test-time scaling
finding: Appending 'Wait' when the model tries to stop (budget forcing) makes it keep reasoning and self-correct.
numbers: s1-32B trained on 1,000 samples; AIME24 from 50% to 57% with budget forcing; abstract claims up to 27% above o1-preview on MATH and AIME24.
limits: Small training set; gain saturates.
agent_relevance: A literal software form of 'persist a few more minutes'. Cheap persistence prompt with a measured gain.

source: Ben-Zion et al. (2025) Assessing and alleviating state anxiety in LLMs (search summary only)
finding: GPT-4 self-reported state anxiety rose after traumatic narratives and fell after mindfulness text, but not to baseline.
numbers: Baseline STAI-s about 31; after narratives 61.6 (accident) to 77.2 (military); after mindfulness 44 +/- 11.
limits: Not opened; no maths-performance outcome measured; authors call 'anxiety' metaphorical.
agent_relevance: Affective text in context can shift LLM outputs; the link to maths accuracy is untested.

source: Hembree (1990) and Ma (1999) math anxiety meta-analyses (cited in Carey 2016)
finding: First two meta-analyses established a robust negative link between maths anxiety and performance.
numbers: r=-0.27 (Hembree) and r=-0.34 (Ma), per Carey et al.
limits: Not opened; pre-2000 samples; correlational.
agent_relevance: Effect size has been stable for 30 years at around -0.3.

source: Wang et al. (2014) genetics of math anxiety (cited in Carey 2016)
finding: Twin analysis: part of math-anxiety variance is genetic, mostly shared with general anxiety.
numbers: About 12% of MA variance linked to maths-cognition genes; most to general anxiety genes (as stated by Carey et al.).
limits: Not opened; secondhand figures.
agent_relevance: Supports a trait-like part of affect; LLM analogue would be model-level baseline, not prompt-level.
